messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur had always found a quiet comfort in order. For forty years as a database administrator, he had built systems of logic and control, worlds where every piece of data had its place and could be retrieved with a precise command. At seventy-eight, divorced and living alone, his small apartment was a reflection of this ethos: books alphabetized, bills filed, a life of predictable inputs and outputs. That predictability shattered six months ago, not with a bang, but with a shallow, rattling breath. What he dismissed as a bad winter cold rapidly descended into a severe pneumonia, then septic shock. He remembers the paramedics, the disorienting blur of the hospital ceiling, and the terrifying helplessness of being intubated in the ICU, his body a battlefield he had no control over.

Since returning home, the order he so carefully curated has been replaced by a pervasive sense of threat. Arthur finds himself constantly on guard, even within the supposed safety of his own home. A car backfiring on the street below makes him jump, his heart hammering against his ribs. He feels a persistent, simmering anger at his own frailty, a deep shame that his body, which he had always taken for granted, could betray him so completely. He is, in his own words, “superalert,” scanning his own physical sensations for the first sign of another collapse. This watchfulness is exhausting, a low-humming dread that underscores every waking moment. This constant state of threat has poisoned his view of the world; he has come to believe it is a fundamentally dangerous place, where disaster can strike without warning. This relentless feeling of being unsafe has also hollowed out his spiritual convictions, leaving him with the desolate feeling that he has lost his faith not just in a higher power, but in the basic benevolence of life itself.

The memories of his time in the hospital are unlike any others he possesses. They are not the hazy recollections of a long-ago holiday but sharp, sensory fragments that feel more real and vivid than the present moment. The smell of bleach from his kitchen sink can instantly trigger an olfactory recall, and he is overwhelmed by the antiseptic scent of the ICU, the sterile air that filled his lungs. In those moments, he feels he is reliving the event, the phantom sensation of the ventilator tube in his throat, the suffocating panic rising in his chest. These intrusive memories are not just frightening; they are evidence. Each time he is pulled back into that hospital bed, it reinforces the terrifying conclusion that his body is his enemy, a volatile system that keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is logically safe in his own living room. The memory proves the appraisal: his own flesh and blood cannot be trusted.

His world has shrunk dramatically. He still does some consulting work from home, but the clean logic of database management now feels like a cruel joke against the chaos he feels inside. The hum of his computer’s cooling fan sometimes sounds too much like the machines that kept him alive, and he has to push his chair back and take deep breaths. He has stopped his daily walks in the park, certain that any exertion could trigger another collapse. Invitations from his few remaining friends are politely declined; the thought of navigating a noisy restaurant, of having to be constantly on guard in public, is more than he can bear. His apartment, once a sanctuary of order, has become a self-imposed prison.

It was his daughter’s visit last week that finally prompted him to seek help. She watched him recoil when she used an antiseptic wipe to clean a small spill, saw the deep, weary lines of vigilance etched around his eyes. He confessed to her that he felt he was waiting for the other shoe to drop, that he couldn’t trust his own body to keep him alive through the night. Arthur came to therapy not with optimism, but with a quiet desperation. He is terrified of spending the last years of his life as a prisoner of his own fear, and holds onto the fragile hope that he might one day feel safe inside his own skin again.
